verdict: Avoid new dye/intermediate exposure in Thane-Belapur until power-demand and output data turn; lend only to specialty players with pass-through contracts and tight monthly discipline.
title: Thane-Belapur Chemicals, Dyes & Intermediates: a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What this business physically is
**A dye or intermediate unit here buys petrochemical and inorganic inputs, runs multi-step batch reactions on steam and power, and sells to textile, agrochemical and pharma buyers.** Cash is made in the reactor, not the warehouse: conversion margin per batch, minus power and effluent cost, minus the working-capital drag of holding inventory across a long reaction chain. Pricing power sits with whoever holds a validated spec with the buyer; commodity dye makers price off Chinese import parity and have none. **So when a proposal lands, check whether the borrower sells on a spec-locked contract or on spot parity; if spot, ask for the last four quarters' realised price versus input cost.**

## What has changed now
**The official data pack reads AVOID at 33 for this cluster, and the local signal is the weak one: Maharashtra electricity demand is up 6.0% Apr-to-date against India's 9.5%, 3.5 pp slower [D].** That is a proxy for how hard the units here are running. Nationally, chemicals output (NIC 20) is -0.5% YoY and -1.2% Apr-to-date [D], while bank credit to the sector is +20.7% YoY [D] — money is chasing a shrinking output base. **So when a proposal lands, check whether the borrower's own sales volume grew or only its borrowing did; if borrowing outran volume, ask why.**

## Where the growth is
**The peer read is unambiguous: Aarti Industries posted Q2 FY27 revenue of ₹3,668 crore, up 75%, and net profit up 58.5%, on 30% volume growth and export demand [3][4].** The growth is in specialty, export-linked, long-term supply agreements — not in commodity dye. Rating commentary flags revenue growth of 3-4% after a 9% dip on Chinese dumping and de-stocking [6], and elevated working-capital intensity in high-growth phases [7].

## How to grow safely
**Structure for the working-capital cycle, because that is where the cash dies: inventory across a multi-step chain plus receivables from textile and agro buyers.** Take monthly stock-and-receivable statements, a charge on current assets, and a covenant capping inventory days; if inventory days rise two months running, ask for the ageing and the buyer-wise outstanding. Insist on a power-cost line in the monthly data — it is the cleanest read on utilisation. **Price the limit to the conversion cycle, not to the borrower's projected turnover.**

## Early warning signs
**Watch the electricity bill and the effluent consent together: falling units with a live consent means the plant is idling, not that demand is soft.** A shift from contract to spot sales, receivable days stretching past the borrower's own stated terms, and any request to fund capex from working-capital limits are the three signals that precede a default here. **If a borrower asks to rephase a limit because a buyer delayed payment, treat it as a receivable-quality event, not a timing event.**
